---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Sustainable Cash After Depreciation Yield
EXPRESSION: RATIO(SUB(oancf, MUL(at, MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
HYPOTHESIS: Operating-cash-flow yield should be rewarded when cash generation remains attractive after charging normalized depreciation for asset consumption.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Cash-flow yield can overstate value when cash flow benefits from noncash depreciation addbacks. Subtracting a smoothed depreciation charge converts cheap cash flow into a more sustainable cash-after-maintenance-accrual yield.
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Industry Adjusted Depreciation Burden EBITDA Trap
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MAX(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che))))), IND_ADJ(RATIO(MUL(at, MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), ADD(ABS(ebitda), ABS(oancf)))))
HYPOTHESIS: High EBITDA-yield firms should underperform when EBITDA cheapness disappears after recognizing an unusually large normalized depreciation burden.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: EBITDA ignores recurring asset consumption, so high EBITDA yield can be a value trap for firms with heavy depreciation requirements. Industry-adjusting the depreciation burden addresses the concern that this channel otherwise just proxies for capital-intensive industry membership.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Persistent Depreciation Conservatism Book
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 5)))
HYPOTHESIS: Book-to-market cheapness should be strongest when recent depreciation intensity is persistently above the firm’s longer-run depreciation norm.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: A one-year depreciation surprise can be noisy, but a sustained elevation in depreciation intensity is more likely to reflect conservative expense recognition. This signal keeps the successful book-value interaction while testing persistence rather than a single-period accounting shock.
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Industry Accrual Reliance Earnings Trap
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), ADD(ABS(ib), ABS(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)))))))
HYPOTHESIS: High earnings-yield firms should underperform when their reported cheapness is unusually accrual-reliant relative to industry peers.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The prior accrual-reliance trap had strong cross-sectional sign alignment but weaker portfolio evidence, suggesting broad industry or sector composition may dilute the spread. Industry-adjusting the reliance leg keeps the short signal focused on cheap firms whose earnings quality is poor relative to comparable accounting environments.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Asset Yield Depreciation Conservatism
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(at, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: Firms cheap relative to their asset base should outperform when current depreciation intensity is above the firm’s recent norm.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel
REASONING: This moves away from another normalization of the book-to-market depreciation signal by using asset-to-market as the valuation leg. The mechanism is that assets priced cheaply are more credible when the firm is currently recognizing asset consumption conservatively rather than flattering earnings through low depreciation.

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Sales Margin Underdepreciation Trap
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RATIO(MUL(sale, SUB(MA(RATIO(dp, sale), 3), RATIO(dp, sale))), ADD(ABS(ib), ABS(oancf))))
HYPOTHESIS: High sales-to-price firms should underperform when reported economics are supported by unusually low depreciation per dollar of sales.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: This is not an industry-adjusted overlay on the earnings-yield underdepreciation trap; it tests whether cheap revenue is paired with artificially boosted margins from low depreciation expense. Scaling the depreciation shortfall by earnings and cash-flow magnitude focuses on economically meaningful margin inflation.

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Abnormal Depreciation Addback Haircut Cash Yield
EXPRESSION: RATIO(SUB(oancf, MAX(SUB(dpc, MA(dpc, 3)), SUB(dpc, dpc))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
HYPOTHESIS: Operating-cash-flow yield should be strongest when current cash flow is not unusually boosted by depreciation and amortization addbacks.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio
REASONING: This avoids collapsing to a standard cash-earnings yield by subtracting only the abnormal excess D&A addback relative to the firm’s own recent history. High scores require cheap operating cash flow that remains attractive after removing a potentially temporary or unusually large noncash addback.

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Depreciation Addback Acceleration EBITDA Trap
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MAX(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che))))), TREND(RATIO(dpc, ADD(ABS(ebitda), ABS(oancf))), 3))
HYPOTHESIS: High EBITDA-yield firms should underperform when dependence on depreciation and amortization addbacks is rising.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel
REASONING: This tests a dynamic deterioration mechanism rather than simply rediscovering EBIT/EV or applying an industry adjustment to a depreciation-burden level. EBITDA cheapness is most suspect when the share of operating performance represented by noncash addbacks is trending upward.

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Cheap Earnings Clean Profitability Decay Trap
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), at), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: High earnings-yield firms should underperform when accrual-adjusted profitability is deteriorating.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: This replaces the static Sloan-style accrual-reliance interaction with a clean-profitability decay mechanism. The signal is high when a firm looks cheap on reported earnings but the trend in accrual-adjusted earnings relative to assets is negative, suggesting the valuation multiple is backward-looking and not cash-supported.
